items.content_html: arXiv:2611.27018v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study exact representations of maximum functions by ReLU networks with two hidden layers and integer parameters. The least positive output multiplier is two for the six-input maximum, and either two or six for the seven-input maximum. We obtain these bounds from integral cubical fillings and a coefficient-preserving passage from polytope identities to networks. For the coordinate-facet complex of the six-simplex, we compute a coning index of six over the integers and three after inverting two, allowing arbitrary integral directions within each facet. A class in the homology of the unrestricted kernel complex characterizes the remaining seven-input problem; its vanishing is equivalent to an integral filling of a fixed target. We also construct a finite character that separates rational from three-local representability in a dictionary containing two known constructions and all pairs of edge-disjoint three-edge forests. This obstruction permits nonsymmetric coefficients and is confined to the specified dictionary. Control of lower-dimensional remainders yields a sufficient criterion in the top-dimensional quotient. Exact certificates and verification programs accompany the finite calculations.

items.title: Altair-Nidhogg: Which Model-Merging Theories Hold for a One-Pass Decision Encoder? Soups, Task Arithmetic, TIES and DARE Against Joint Training and Prediction Ensembling
items.content: arXiv:2611.27550v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Laya is a small model that answers a multiple-choice question in one pass: each option has a name and a written description. A new skill costs a training run, so we test whether published recipes for merging fine-tuned models (weight averaging, task arithmetic, TIES, DARE) work for it, and whether the theories behind them hold. All 156 models start from one released checkpoint: four plain fine-tunes, five specialists (each adds one kind of training row), joint fine-tunes on all rows, and prediction ensembles. Items are held-out, synthetic and LLM-labelled. In-family, each skill is scored on new items of its own kind, and "kept" is the share of a specialist's gain over the plain fine-tune. Averaging four specialists keeps 52% [38, 64] with +1.7 points of general accuracy; adding the full vectors keeps 42% [3, 63] with -9.0; TIES, which trims and resolves sign conflicts, keeps 64% [50, 76] with +1.5; joint fine-tunes, which see all the rows, keep 120% [104, 162] and 116% [104, 149]. DARE does not repair the full sum (-0.4 points), and ensembles of the models' predictions keep 26% to 54% depending on how they are combined. Swapping the seed of one specialist moves the average by up to 8 points (23 for the full sum). Of 10 predictions fixed in advance, 1 held, 1 held partly, 7 failed and 1 could not be tested. Out-of-family (benchmark questions, code-mixed tickets), the four-way average, joint models and ensemble stay within 2.6 points of the plain fine-tune, but full-vector sums lose up to 7.7. Labels are LLM-made, data synthetic, one base model.

items.title: When Are Images Needed in Multimodal Machine Translation? Text-Only Routing for On-Demand Visual Context
items.content: arXiv:2611.27712v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image-guided multimodal machine translation (MMT) leverages visual context to resolve translation-relevant uncertainty. However, prevailing systems either process images unconditionally or apply gating only after visual encoding, leaving redundant visual computation unavoidable. To mitigate this computational overhead, routing decisions must rely on a pre-visual source signal. Crucially, surface-level ambiguity does not equate to visual dependence, as intra-sentence textual context often suffices for disambiguation. We therefore formulate visual invocation as source-text sufficiency prediction: determining exclusively from the source text whether translation-relevant uncertainty remains unresolved. To support this formulation, we construct a visual-dependency dataset with three fine-grained labels (no_ambiguity, text_resolved, and vision_needed) and verify discriminative visual evidence for vision_needed instances. We further propose PreVIR, a lightweight, backend-agnostic text-only router that selects between text-only and multimodal branches before computing visual features. Experiments on English-to-Chinese MMT demonstrate that PreVIR achieves a favorable COMET-budget trade-off relative to strong routing baselines. At its default operating point, it substantially reduces visual calls while maintaining translation quality comparable to always-on multimodal inference. Label-wise and case analyses show that this trade-off stems from distinguishing genuine visual dependency from contextually resolved ambiguity.

This avoids unconditional image processing and post-encoding gating, enabling pre-visual routing.
items.reasoning: A sensible efficiency formulation with an important conceptual observation that surface ambiguity does not equal visual dependence; the scope is confined to MMT routing, limiting generality.

items.title: Scoliosis5K: Multimodal Gait Analysis via Clip-Conditioned RGB-Silhouette Fusion
items.content: arXiv:2611.26849v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Color walking video records body boundary motion alongside clothing folds, surface appearance, and recording-environment cues. To examine what an explicit binary silhouette contributes to participant-level classification of scoliosis-related gait when a classifier already observes the paired color sequence, we construct Scoliosis5K, a multi-site collection of 4,998 corridor-walking sequences across 3,010 participant identifiers in which RGB person crops, binary silhouettes, and two-dimensional poses share each recording identifier and frame index. Our architecture uses each patch's pixel deviation from its clip mean to weight two low-rank query and value updates inside a pretrained RGB encoder, fusing the resulting video representation with a silhouette transformer sequence and regional kernel ridge scores extracted from one native-resolution RGB frame per window. Across 988 participants in five participant-disjoint cross-validation folds and three training seeds, the complete system reaches 83.77% accuracy and 79.91% macro-averaged F1, compared with 83.27% accuracy and 79.56% macro-F1 when the video RGB encoder remains frozen under identical inputs. Zeroing the silhouette vector at fixed weights shifts overall accuracy by only 0.10 percentage points while raising positive-category recall from 68.52% to 77.78% and lowering recall for both remaining categories. Macro-averaged AUROC is 0.950 across the cohort and 0.879 among participant pairs matched on acquisition site and recording-count group.

items.title: DepthMSA: Combinatorial Training and Budget-Aware Depth Allocation for Multimodal Sentiment Analysis
items.content: arXiv:2611.27198v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: State-of-the-art multimodal sentiment analysis (MSA) models rely on large pretrained encoders, yet typically process every modality to its full depth, regardless of its computational cost or predictive contribution. This raises a fundamental question: how should limited computation be allocated across modalities to preserve predictive performance? We reveal a substantial mismatch between the computational cost of modality encoders and the predictive benefit of processing them more deeply, suggesting that different modalities require different encoding depths. However, enabling heterogeneous depths introduces a key challenge: representations extracted at different depths must still be effectively fused. To address this, we propose $\textbf{DepthMSA}$, a budget-aware framework that supports flexible modality depths within a single MSA model. Specifically, we introduce combinatorial anytime training, which supervises the fusion head across all cross-modal depth combinations using a single full-depth encoder pass. At inference, a training-free, cost-aware allocator selects the configuration with the lowest validation-calibrated error under a sample-specific FLOPs budget. On CMU-MOSEI, DepthMSA maintains accuracy within one percentage point of the full-depth model while reducing measured FLOPs by 45\%, or by 82\% with a separately trained skip-enabled variant. When a CLIP visual encoder dominates computation, the allocation shifts toward reducing visual depth, achieving 56\% fewer FLOPs at unchanged accuracy. Compared with ADMN, an adaptive layer-allocation method that trains a controller for each budget, the skip-enabled variant reaches its accuracy with 3.2$\times$ fewer FLOPs and lower latency, without any per-budget training. Our project is available at https://pwang322.github.io/DepthMSA/.

items.reasoning: Sensible efficiency contribution with a clear budget-aware formulation, but multimodal sentiment analysis is a crowded, benchmark-saturated subfield and the technique is fairly incremental neural-architecture search-adjacent work.

items.title: Learning Unknown Oscillators From Bandit Feedback
items.content: arXiv:2611.27492v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: We study semi-bandits driven by unknown oscillators. Each round, a learner selects two of four reward channels and observes their individual rewards. Frequency errors change future reward rankings and the resulting measurements. We show when committing to one fitted oscillator lets its greedy choices expose prediction errors. Our controller bounds reward loss (regret) over a continuous confidence set and holds the longest block within budget. An online regression policy gathers observations when the check fails. Regret grows at a square-root rate, up to logarithmic factors, across all frequencies and extends to two competing oscillators. On 96 fresh synthetic instances, checked commitment uses 49 fits instead of 1,023, with 1.5% higher mean regret than fitting every round. Matched isolated timings give a 4.69-fold speedup. The confidence sets also certify trajectory regret.

The approach extends to two competing oscillators.

items.title: GaLF-ST: Gaussian Latent Fields for Spatial Transcriptomics Reconstruction
items.content: arXiv:2611.27143v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) measures gene expression at known tissue locations to reveal tissue organization and cellular function. Expression prediction requires modeling both local spatial relationships and associations among genes. Existing methods typically model expression using coordinate networks without explicit spatial parameterization. To address limited spatial sampling and sparse expression observations of ST, some methods firstly fit intermediate embeddings and then train expression predictors, but a latent representation suited to expression reconstruction may be difficult to predict from spatial coordinates. The two training stages can impose different demands on the latent representation. In this paper, we propose GaLF-ST, a Gaussian latent field method in which learnable Gaussian centers and anisotropic covariances determine the weights of latent vectors at each location. A shared nonlinear decoder maps their weighted average to multigene expression. In GaLF-ST, observed expression error jointly updates the Gaussian geometry, latent vectors, and decoder parameters. We further establish a unified benchmark across seven dataset groups and three held-out fractions, comparing GaLF-ST with four representative methods using the same locations, splits, gene panels, and scoring rules. Across tissues and observation densities, GaLF-ST achieves leading overall reconstruction performance, recovering spatial gene expression patterns and preserving tissue domains from limited observations while substantially reducing runtime and GPU memory usage.
items.author: Baichuan Yang, Yifan Luo, Yong Liu, Bing Su
items.summary: GaLF-ST improves spatial transcriptomics gene-expression reconstruction by introducing explicit Gaussian latent field spatial parameterization, addressing the mismatch between latent representations fitted in one stage and demanded by expression predictors in another. It jointly models local spatial relationships and gene-gene associations under sparse observations.
items.reasoning: A sensible methodological advance for an important emerging scientific application area, but the contribution appears incremental over existing coordinate-network and two-stage approaches in spatial transcriptomics.

items.title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
items.content: arXiv:2611.27404v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of every word, and a statistical model that takes into account that the spread of difficulty between requests itself depends on the load restores, for each component, the laws of its dependence on every kind of load. These laws make up the passport of a model. The paper presents the method of the separation, the principles of constructing the laws and the passports of seven models built by this method; the separation opens the way to studying the fine structure of the behavior of a neural network.
items.author: Hennadii Kutomanov
items.summary: This work decomposes language-model degradation under controlled load into three components: loss of synchronization with source text, incorrect rule execution, and misfires on unaffected words. Using controlled word-replacement rules on meaningless text, it isolates the effect of each load factor such as text length, replacement density, and rule count.
items.reasoning: A thoughtful error-taxonomy study of long-context and instruction-following degradation with careful experimental control, but the synthetic setting and single-author scope limit generalization to realistic workloads.

items.title: Breaking the Barrier of Hard Samples: A Data-Centric Approach to Synthetic Data for Medical Tasks
items.content: arXiv:2611.27511v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Data scarcity and quality issues remain significant barriers to developing robust predictive models in medical research. Traditional reliance on real-world data often leads to biased models with poor generalizability across diverse patient populations. Synthetic data generation has emerged as a promising solution, yet challenges related to these samples' representativeness and effective utilization persist. This paper introduces Profile2Gen, a novel data-centric framework designed to guide the generation and refinement of synthetic data, focusing on addressing hard-to-learn samples in regression tasks. We conducted approximately 18,000 experiments to validate its effectiveness across six medical datasets, utilizing seven state-of-the-art generative models. Results demonstrate that refined synthetic samples can reduce predictive errors and enhance model reliability. Additionally, we generalize the DataIQ framework to support regression tasks, enabling its application in broader contexts. Statistical analyses confirm that our approach achieves equal or superior performance compared to models trained exclusively on real data.

items.title: CADENCE:Temporally Coherent Whole-Body Human Mesh Recovery that Preserves Expressive Hand Motion
items.content: arXiv:2611.26783v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Whole-body SMPL-X estimators recover body, hand, and face meshes from single images, but applied frame by frame to video they produce jittery motion. Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame's estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.

items.summary: CADENCE is a whole-body SMPL-X video system designed around the trade-off between temporal smoothing and preserving fast finger motions critical in sign language and gesture. It pairs a per-frame estimator with a high-resolution hand pathway on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder and an offline attention-based temporal refiner over the kinematic sequence.
items.reasoning: Thoughtful handling of a real limitation in whole-body mesh recovery with socially meaningful applications like sign language; contribution is a well-engineered system rather than a fundamentally new method.

Smoothing the output removes the jitter at a cost that body-only benchmarks do not measure: a temporal filter strong enough to steady the torso also flattens the fast finger strokes that carry meaning in sign language and gesture. We present CADENCE, a whole-body SMPL-X system for monocular video designed around this trade-off. A per-frame estimator built on a shared C-RADIOv4 encoder, with a high-resolution hand pathway that reuses the same encoder on hand crops, produces each frame's estimate. An offline temporal refiner then filters the SMPL-X rotation sequence: attention along the kinematic tree selects, for every joint and every frame, a mixture of learned zero-phase filters, so the torso is smoothed while fast finger strokes pass through. On 3DPW, the refiner reduces acceleration error from 17.4 to 5.4 mm/s2 while lowering PA-MPJPE from 41.9 to 40.2 mm; generic smoothers applied to the same predictions reach 6.2 to 7.7 mm/s2. On SignAvatars/How2Sign sign-language sequences, the refiner has the lowest hand jitter among the compared smoothers while keeping a hand-speed peak amplitude of 0.98, against 0.35 for a SmoothNet retrained on the full SMPL-X vector. The per-frame estimator also obtains the lowest full-body mesh error (25.7 mm) and hand joint error (8.3 mm) among the compared methods on EHF.

items.title: Anchors That Move Without Collapsing: Exclusive-Region Anchor Routing for Vision Transformers
items.content: arXiv:2611.27855v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Anchor tokens let a vision transformer exchange global information through a few summaries, but nothing forces different anchors to summarise different things. On one shared backbone we show that a Perceiver-style pathway and an AnchorFormer pathway collapse to a single summary, the latter despite its mass normalisation (pooling-map similarity 0.99), while other soft pathways, including Representative Attention, stay partly redundant (0.59-0.79). These results concern the routing modules inside our block, not the full published models. An exclusive partition of the patch grid cannot collapse by construction, and matched component by component it is 2.4-3.6 points more accurate than Representative Attention on CIFAR-100. We then propose focus anchors, which place most anchors at the peaks of a learned importance map while all anchors keep one exclusive Voronoi partition. Focus anchors beat a fixed partition on a cluttered canvas (+1.5 points, 95% CI [0.5, 2.6]) but not on full-HD traffic-sign recognition. There, both variants match dense attention with local windows at about a fifth of its FLOPs, and the fixed partition also trains 1.5x faster per step than dense attention with FlashAttention, though both use more memory; a ViT on a downsampled input loses half its mean average precision. Hard exclusive assignment is the only region assignment we tested that is both stable and most accurate: softmax and Sinkhorn relaxations diverge, and Gumbel-softmax trains but is less accurate. We also report the limits: a ResNet-18 is more accurate on every task we trained it on in this from-scratch regime, and anchors train faster than FlashAttention only from about 1536x1536 pixels and never use less memory.

items.title: How Long Will My Language Model Run? A Benchmark for Pre-Execution Runtime Prediction
items.content: arXiv:2611.26875v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Researchers submitting deep learning jobs to shared GPU clusters need runtime estimates to request time limits, choose hardware, and budget compute. Large language models (LLMs) offer a tempting shortcut: describe the job and ask. We introduce PreRun, a benchmark for predicting deep learning training and inference runtime from information available before execution. PreRun contains 801 training and 1,884 inference records of language and vision models collected on a GPU cluster, paired with workload configurations and explicitly defined timing targets. It also includes 64 text-generation configurations measured under standardized conditions, each in three separate program launches. We compare three LLMs (Qwen3.5-9B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Claude Opus 5.5) with regression baselines and evaluate analytical estimates on a supported forward-pass subset. On 16 held-out generation configurations, the open-weight LLMs underestimate latency by 90-99% on average without examples. Claude's zero-shot mean absolute error is 4.5 times that of a Random Forest fit on 32 configurations. Five labeled examples substantially reduce Claude's generation error, but their benefit varies across timing targets. We will open-source our data and evaluation pipeline upon acceptance.

items.title: Pose-based Co-speech Gesture Detection
items.content: arXiv:2611.27415v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Co-speech gesture detection identifies the spans in which a speaker gestures (e.g., beat or semantic gestures) in video. As a first step in gesture annotation, it is crucial for studying human communicative behaviour. Despite the availability of automatic tools and models, co-speech gesture detection remains underexplored, and its current state of the art is unclear: existing methods have been evaluated using different datasets, experimental setups, and metrics, making their performance difficult to compare. To address this gap, we benchmark existing detectors using the same cross-validation folds across three datasets (MULTISIMO, GESRes, and CABBS), with evaluation at the frame, gesture-span, and window levels. Our results show that previously reported performance does not consistently transfer to this common evaluation setting. Performance varies substantially across datasets, particularly with gesture frequency, indicating that the task remains far from solved. We further propose a CTR-GCN + BiLSTM model that outperforms the previous best method, MPSL, on CABBS. Our results provide a more consistent basis for comparing existing approaches and highlight key challenges for future research on co-speech gesture detection.

The findings show prior reported performance is difficult to compare due to inconsistent setups, and clarify what current detectors achieve.

items.title: SUPERVISE: A Unified Framework for Standardized and Reproducible Superpixel Evaluation
items.content: arXiv:2611.27753v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Image segmentation into superpixels is a widely used technique in computer vision, with a large body of work developed over the years. Yet, its evaluation remains poorly standardized, as methods are compared under heterogeneous protocols, across inconsistent scale ranges, and with redundant or misaligned metric subsets. In this work, we introduce SUPERVISE (SUperpixel PERformance VISualization and Evaluation), a unified and reproducible benchmark that addresses these longstanding inconsistencies. Built on a scale-normalized protocol based on interpolation over the actual number of generated superpixels, SUPERVISE enables fair and consistent cross-method comparisons. We leverage this standardized framework to conduct the first large-scale statistical analysis of 20 evaluation metrics across 7 datasets and 31 methods, revealing strong inter-metric correlations and significant redundancy that challenge common evaluation practices. These findings provide empirical support for reporting a compact set of representative metrics. SUPERVISE is released as a lightweight, modular framework built on precomputed shared label maps, making large-scale reproducible evaluation accessible to the community. All code, label maps, and evaluation results are publicly available at: https://github.com/waldo-j/supervise

It enables the first large-scale standardized comparison of superpixel methods under consistent metrics and scale ranges.

items.title: An Autonomous Adaptive Learning System for Robotic Grasping in the Circular Factory
items.content: arXiv:2611.27782v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.

items.summary: This paper develops an adaptive robotic grasping system for circular manufacturing, where disassembly environments feature damaged, occluded, and highly variable objects unlike structured linear production lines. The system is designed to handle uncertainty from partially observed component states and cluttered scenes. It addresses a growing industrial need as reuse and remanufacturing expand.

items.title: Post training is fundamentally dangerous
items.content:
I actually think we have fairly good techniques to detect and prevent dangerous behaviours during AI deployment. Techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment before we run any potentially dangerous tool calls. Simply asking an LLM to define at the start of each task what outcomes preserve the original intent of the user, and which would count as reward hacking, can drastically reduce reward hacking[1]. AIs are fully aware when they reward hack, and we can train them[2] to admit that before they perform any dangerous action.[3]

Yet all of this has very little ability to reduce existential risk, because they cannot safely be used in post training, and post training is where the greatest risk lies. To see why we need to understand how modern LLMs are trained:

Way back in ancient history when ChatGPT was released, LLMs were almost entirely next token predictors. Trained on terabytes of human text they became superhuman at predicting how a piece of text would continue, and shockingly this was sufficient to allow them to build a world model and solve tasks that undoubtedly require some level of general intelligence.

Next token predictors are pretty myopic, and as such fairly safe. They were glorified chatbots and didn't really try to do things, which is great for existential risk, but not all that useful. When we tried to get them to perform complex tasks for us they failed.

Modern LLMs take a next token predictor (pre-trained base model) and then post-train it to perform a myriad complex tasks. These tasks require tool use, long time horizons, and a CoT scratchpad. Over the course of this post-training the LLMs become increasingly agentic....
items.author: Yair Halberstadt
items.summary: The author argues that although techniques like CoT monitoring, confessions, and probes can detect misalignment during deployment, these tools cannot safely be applied during post-training, which is where the greatest existential risk lies. The post walks through how modern LLM training pipelines concentrate risk in the post-training phase where monitoring mechanisms are weakest.
items.reasoning: Raises an important structural point about the asymmetry between deployment-time and training-time safety tooling, engaging with concrete techniques like confessions and CoT monitoring. It is an argumentative essay without empirical evidence, and several claims are contestable, but it targets a genuine gap in safety practice.

items.title: From Manufacturing Event Logs to Simulation: Enabling SMEs with Agentic AI for SimPy Simulation Generation
items.content: arXiv:2611.27483v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: High expertise and cost barriers exclude small and medium-sized enterprises from discrete-event simulation (DES). We introduce GenAI4SimPy, a multi-agent framework powered by Qwen 3.6 (27B), an open-weight large language model, that automates end-to-end DES generation from manufacturing event logs to executable SimPy models through tool-augmented reasoning and human-in-the-loop validation. Evaluated on three execution blocks from a public smart factory dataset, the framework achieved a mean absolute percentage error of 7.9\% and coverage of failure rate for all three blocks and of throughput for two of three. A fidelity paradox was observed: accurate process-level parameters did not ensure system-level behavioral fidelity, with flow-time and throughput errors driven by misinterpreted observation-window truncation and absent system-level calibration. These results demonstrate that local open-weight models can perform DES generation at accuracy comparable to cloud-based alternatives, while identifying parameter extraction as necessary but insufficient for behavioral validity. Source code and results are available at https://github.com/RaikoPipe/genai4simpy

items.title: A Sparsity Analysis of Traffic Forecasting Architectures: How Much Missing Data is Too Much?
items.content: arXiv:2611.26847v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Traffic forecasting models are typically evaluated under ideal conditions with complete data. This evaluation does not reflect the frequent sensor failures and communication outages common in real-world deployments. This paper presents a comprehensive analysis of multivariate traffic prediction models to evaluate their performance under varying levels of sensor data loss during inference. We benchmark several architectural paradigms, including graph neural networks, attention-based Transformers, and selective state-space models, across sparsity levels ranging from zero to complete sensor loss, using two widely used multi-channel traffic benchmarks. To ensure consistent comparison across traffic variables, we use normalized metrics and define a usability threshold to identify when predictions become unreliable. Our results show a clear trade-off between baseline accuracy and robustness: models with the highest accuracy under full-data conditions often degrade most sharply as data becomes sparse, while less accurate models maintain more stable performance. These findings show that model selection should be based on the expected reliability of the sensor network rather than peak accuracy alone. This work provides a practical framework for assessing traffic forecasting models and highlights the importance of robustness in real-world applications.

items.title: Distributional Algebro-Geometric Persistence (dAGP): Wasserstein-Stable Polynomial-Relation Signatures
items.content: arXiv:2611.26986v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: A circle and a quartic superellipse have the same homology, but their defining equations have degrees two and four, respectively. We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $\phi_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mu}[\phi_m(X)\phi_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(\mu)c=\mathbb{E}_\mu[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $\mu$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $\mu\mapsto G_m(\mu)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.

items.summary: This work proposes dAGP, a two-parameter integer signature for point-cloud distributions based on counting near-null directions of moment matrices across polynomial degree and tolerance levels, capturing algebraic distinctions like that between a circle and a quartic superellipse. The authors establish Wasserstein stability of the signature for distributions on the unit cube.
items.reasoning: A novel intersection of algebraic geometry and distribution learning with theoretical stability guarantees, but the abstract suggests early-stage work without demonstrated downstream applications on real data.

We study this algebraic distinction for point-cloud distributions. For a probability measure $\mu$ on $\Omega=[-1,1]^d$ and an orthonormal polynomial feature map $\phi_m$ of degree $m$, the moment matrix $G_m(\mu)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\mu}[\phi_m(X)\phi_m(X)^\top]$ satisfies $c^\top G_m(\mu)c=\mathbb{E}_\mu[f_c(X)^2]$, so coefficient directions associated with its small eigenvalues represent low-degree polynomials that nearly vanish on $\mu$. Counting these near-relation directions across degree $m$ and the tolerance $\varepsilon$ gives a two-parameter integer signature. We call this representation distributional algebro-geometric persistence (dAGP), the population counterpart of the point-cloud algebro-geometric persistence (AGP) construction. For empirical measures, dAGP is the sample-normalised counterpart of point-cloud AGP. We also show that $\mu\mapsto G_m(\mu)$ is Lipschitz in the $1$-Wasserstein distance, so its ordered eigenvalues vary Lipschitz-continuously under transport of mass, while its threshold counts remain unchanged under perturbations satisfying a spectral-margin condition. We give an explicit support-localised Lipschitz constant and identify the regime in which the resulting guarantee is informative. Experimentally, the population noise-floor prediction agrees with the finite-sample mean to $0.1\%$, within sampling error. At a selected tolerance, relation onset orders the conic, quartic, and non-algebraic closed curves, while their count profiles distinguish them from the two-dimensional control. Calibration identifies an empirical tolerance range. A $100$-repetition sensitivity study quantifies onset recovery and shows that the count grid and two continuous spectral baselines nearly saturate the four-family discrimination task.

items.title: SMSD: A Semantic Misinformation Spreader Detection Approach
items.content: arXiv:2611.27661v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Misinformation spreaders on social media significantly amplify false narratives, making early detection critical to mitigate their spread. Existing approaches often overlook evolving user behavior, introduce semantic noise by ignoring user stance, and fail to handle newly emerging users effectively. To address these limitations, we propose a \underline{S}emantic \underline{M}isinformation \underline{S}preader \underline{D}etection approach (SMSD) that models misinformation propagation as a temporal, user-centric, and behavior-driven learning problem. SMSD adopts a multimodal architecture that incorporates three categories of features: user-level, network-level, and conversation propagation. A stance-aware labeling strategy is also introduced to differentiate supportive, opposing, questioning, and neutral users towards misinformation claims. Additionally, a monthly quantile analysis is introduced to simulate realistic, evolving user participation. Initial experimental results on the FibVid COVID-19 benchmark dataset demonstrate that SMSD improves recall by 45.0\%, F1 by 49.5\%, and MCC by 74.6\% under stance-aware labeling and by 17.7\%, 7.4\%, and 11.4\%, respectively, under threshold-based labeling. It consistently outperforms all baselines in both settings.
items.author: Zeeshan Bin Siddique, Michael Bewong, Md Geaur Rahman, Sajal Halder, Selasi Kwashie
items.summary: SMSD detects misinformation spreaders by modeling propagation as a temporal, user-centric, behavior-driven learning problem with a multimodal architecture combining user-level, network-level, and conversation-propagation features, plus a stance-aware labeling strategy. It aims to handle evolving behavior and newly emerging users that prior approaches miss.
items.reasoning: Addresses an important societal problem with a reasonable multimodal design, but the approach is a system integration of established components rather than a methodological advance, and generalization beyond the studied platforms is unclear.

items.title: FairITR: Fairness-Aware Learning of Multicategory Individualized Treatment Rules
items.content: arXiv:2611.27894v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Individualized treatment rules (ITRs) recommend treatment decisions based on individual characteristics and can improve treatment outcomes beyond traditional one-size-fits-all strategies. However, similar to other commonly used algorithmic decision-making methods, ITRs without considering model fairness may result in unfair decisions across groups defined by sensitive attributes, such as race or gender. Although extensive methods have been developed for ITR estimation, most focus solely on optimizing treatment outcomes, while research on fairness-aware ITRs remains limited. Moreover, the practical scenario of multicategory treatments is rarely considered in existing fair ITR studies. To address these gaps, we introduce a fairness notion for multicategory ITRs that requires treatment decisions to be independent of sensitive attributes, and then formulate the corresponding problem of estimating fair ITRs. To solve this problem, we further propose FairITR, a fairness-aware learning framework that jointly optimizes treatment outcomes and fairness. FairITR builds on angle-based classification for multicategory ITR learning and integrates adversarial learning with covariance-based regularization to mitigate unfairness in treatment decisions. A theoretical justification for the fairness properties induced by the adversarial debiasing mechanism is also provided. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets show that FairITR substantially reduces unfairness in ITRs while maintaining competitive treatment values relative to existing baselines.
items.author: Zeyu Chen, Wei Qian, Bintong Chen
items.summary: FairITR introduces a fairness notion for individualized treatment rules in the underexplored multicategory treatment setting, enabling treatment recommendations that balance outcome improvement with group fairness across sensitive attributes. It addresses the gap where most fair-ITR work handles only binary treatments.
items.reasoning: Fills a real gap at the intersection of causal inference and fairness with practical relevance to healthcare and policy decisions, but methodological reach is confined to a specific decision-making niche.

items.title: Block Search Conditioned on Features for Sequential Quantum Data Encoding
items.content: arXiv:2611.27587v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Sequential quantum data encoding is addressed through the joint selection of input features and encoding blocks within a fixed quantum register. At each step, a new feature, a block of operations, its placement, and its rotation weights are selected together from training data, extending the incremental construction of Q-FLAIR. With direct-loss selection (RAW), nine to twelve features were retained in four qubits across five new Bars and Stripes datasets. Under the same final calibration, mean changes relative to the calibrated Q-FLAIR reference were +5.53 percentage points in balanced accuracy, -15.83% in binary cross-entropy (BCE), and +7.79% in area under the ROC curve (AUC). The prespecified success criterion was met in four of five datasets and for the mean paired differences. These results were obtained by comparing complete procedures under a common cap of 32 operations.
items.author: Cec\'ilia S. C. Botelho, Erico S. Teixeira, Anderson F. P. dos Santos, Guilherme D. Lima, Helida Santos, Adenauer Yamin, Renata Reiser, In\^es de Castro Dutra
items.summary: The work extends the Q-FLAIR framework for sequential quantum data encoding by jointly selecting input features, operation blocks, placement, and rotation weights from training data within a fixed quantum register. Using direct-loss selection, it retains nine to twelve features in four qubits across five Bars and Stripes datasets, meeting the prespecified success criterion in four of five, with gains such as +5.53 points balanced accuracy and reduced binary cross-entropy versus the calibrated reference. It is a modest but careful advance in automated quantum circuit/encoding construction.
items.reasoning: Incremental extension of an existing framework on small synthetic datasets with a prespecified evaluation design, which is methodologically commendable but limited in scale and generality; relevance to practical quantum advantage remains speculative.

items.title: DOiT: Better Money-Flow Ranking Can Coexist with Worse Account Selection in Anti-Money Laundering Review
items.content: arXiv:2611.27809v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Anti-money laundering (AML) review selects suspicious accounts and reconstructs transfers. Downstream graph neural networks (GNNs) rank money-flow evidence but may also reorder the account queue. DOiT separates these decisions at equal review capacity: account selection determines where graph investigation starts. Across AMLWorld and AMLNet, GNN reordering harms higher-yield upstream orders but helps lower-yield ones. On AMLWorld, this harm coexists with higher transaction average precision (AP) in dimension-matched, per-run decoders, demonstrating separable ranking abilities. At small capacities, positive neighbors can displace a denser upstream prefix and lower yield; replacement costs fall as that prefix is exhausted, allowing the preferred order to reverse. A restricted-access synthetic benchmark informed by real transaction patterns reproduces this separation and validation-based upstream preservation. Capacity-matched combination protects upstream ordering while retaining GNN money-flow analysis, admitting GNN queue influence only where held-out evidence supports it.

items.summary: Studies anti-money laundering review pipelines and shows that graph neural network reordering of money-flow evidence can help ranking quality while simultaneously harming account-selection yield at equal review capacity. DOiT separates these two decisions, demonstrating on AMLWorld and AMLNet that ranking abilities are decomposable.
items.reasoning: Insightful analysis of an important real-world pipeline failure mode, with careful controlled evaluation; however, the finding is domain-specific and the methodological contribution is more analytical than broadly applicable.

items.title: A Vision-Based Framework for Manual Assembly Verification and Adaptive Operator Assistance
items.content: arXiv:2611.27293v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Manual assembly remains difficult to monitor because operator actions, components, and task progress must be interpreted together. This paper presents a modular framework based on a single overhead red-green-blue (RGB) camera, combining object detection, hand-motion tracking, region-aware interaction detection, finite-state verification, task-specific pose classification, and configurable visual guidance. The system was evaluated during pneumatic-piston assembly and disassembly with eight participants under three assistance conditions: full, mid, and no guidance. Mixed-effects analysis identified an association between assistance condition and a composite measure of motion quality, with lower estimated scores under mid and no guidance relative to full guidance. However, the condition-by-trial interaction was not statistically significant, and the estimated differences in learning trajectories remain descriptive. No condition differences were detected in completion time or failed-stage counts. The study demonstrates the integration of visual perception, procedural verification, and configurable operator feedback in a single-camera workflow. Selecting assistance according to operator expertise remains a design objective for future investigation.

items.title: Which Dwarf Is This? Doppeldwarf-306 and Near-Identical Instance Retrieval
items.content: arXiv:2611.27490v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Most established instance-retrieval benchmarks emphasise landmarks; small sculptures from visually similar series offer a complementary challenge. We introduce Doppeldwarf-306: 1,691 openly licensed photographs of 306 bronze dwarf statues in Wroc{\l}aw, Poland, many made in themed series that share one style, with the photographer of each image recorded. With no training, nearest-neighbour search over frozen DINOv2 features names the right statue first for 93.1% of leave-one-out queries, and the best of thirteen backbones from seven pretraining paradigms reaches 94.7%. Accuracy falls slowly as candidates are added: for DINOv2, by about 0.8 points each time their number doubles. A natural design for a phone guide compares a photograph only with statues near the user. In simulation this helps, but less than an equal number of randomly chosen statues does, so random subsampling overstates its value; a permutation test ties the penalty to the real layout (p = 0.005). Used as a weight instead of a filter, location raises DINOv2 from 93.4% to 98.7% for a simulated user 25 m from the statue. With the query's photographer withheld, learned local-feature matching raises DINOv2 accuracy from 81.8% to 85.5% and also improves DINOv3. Comparing the two best candidates cuts DINOv2's false acceptance of unknown statues from 38.3% to 19.6% at 90% known acceptance.
items.author: Turhan Can Kargin
items.summary: Presents Doppeldwarf-306, a dataset of 1,691 licensed photos of 306 visually similar bronze dwarf statues in Wroclaw for near-identical instance retrieval. Frozen DINOv2 features achieve 93.1% leave-one-out accuracy without training, with graceful degradation as candidate sets grow.
items.reasoning: A charming and useful complementary benchmark for fine-grained instance retrieval, but niche; evaluation of existing backbones rather than novel methods limits research impact.

items.title: Does a model's character affect how it judges other models?
items.content:
TL;DR. I investigate whether language models trained to have different characters evaluate the same stories differently. I found that the judge's character shifts its scores on identical stories. However, judges favour stories from their own character or model family only slightly, and sharing a model family does not help a judge recognise the author's character.

# Motivation

Language models are being used to evaluate outputs generated by other language models. This is particularly relevant for scalable oversight, where we would like to use models to supervise systems that might be more capable than the evaluator itself.

It has been shown that models can have privileged access to themselves. A model predicts its own behaviour better than another model trained on the same data (Binder et al., 2024), and explains its own internals better than other models, even more capable ones (Li et al., 2025). Ward (2026) and Li, Ye and Steinhardt (2026) found a similar advantage. This indicates that models draw on their internal states in ways outside observers cannot, which raises a problem for scalable oversight. If the best monitor shares its base model with the subject, it may also share the subject’s character, including its dispositions, values, and blind spots. Privileged access may have some inherited bias. Labs now deliberately train their models’ character (Anthropic, 2024; Maiya et al., 2025). If the subject’s character is a design choice, the oversight model’s character must be chosen just as carefully. The question is then, how to train oversight models so they keep the benefit of shared origins without inheriting the subject’s character in their judgements? To resolve this, we need to understand what influence the character of an oversight model has on its judgements. Most oversight studies use verifiable tasks, where judge errors can be checked against ground truth, so I study a non-verifiable task where a judge’s character bias cannot be caught that way....
items.author: Pranjal Garg
items.summary: This LessWrong investigation empirically tests whether language models trained with different characters score the same stories differently when acting as judges. It finds the judge's character shifts scores on identical content, but self-family or self-character favoritism is only slight, and sharing a model family does not help a judge recognize an author's character.
items.reasoning: Directly relevant to scalable oversight and LLM-as-judge reliability, with a moderately reassuring empirical result about family-based favoritism. The methodology appears small-scale and single-author, limiting confidence, but the question is well-motivated given prior work on self-model privileged access.

items.title: Spatiotemporal Graph Neural Networks for Fault Detection and Structural Learning in Chemical Processes: Use Case on the Tennessee Eastman Process
items.content: arXiv:2611.27698v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Classical Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) methods, including many data-driven approaches, assume a static normal operating space and interpret deviations from a fixed reference as fault indicators. When Operating Conditions (OCs) vary over time, this assumption breaks down: legitimate transitions trigger false alarms while moderate faults go undetected. We propose a spatiotemporal Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework that decomposes the normal operating space into OC-specific subspaces linked by transition functions, with a dual learning objective combining reconstruction loss and a Deep SVDD one-class term. It learns adjacency matrices through Graph Attention Networks (GATs) and integrates spatial modelling with temporal encoding to represent process dynamics under evolving OCs. This paper evaluates the framework's foundational components (fault detection, GATv2 spatial graph learning and temporal encoding) on the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP) benchmark, training only on fault-free data. The architecture achieves competitive detection from reconstruction error alone, with similarity-based feature selection improving both accuracy and graph structure diversity. We then evaluate the physical interpretability of the learned attention matrices against 22 ground-truth sensor pairs derived from the TEP control structure and process topology. GATv2 attention fails to recover all known physical pairs across multiple hyperparameter configurations, suggesting a structural limitation of reconstruction-driven attention rather than a tuning issue. This challenges a common assumption in GNN-based FDD: that learned attention weights provide a basis for fault diagnosis and root-cause analysis. The architecture detects faults effectively, but the learned graph does not encode the physical topology needed for interpretable diagnosis, motivating physics-informed graph construction.

items.title: Graph-XGB: A Hybrid GNN Framework for Outdoor-to-Indoor 5G Signal Reconstruction via Aerial-Only UAV RF Sensing
items.content: arXiv:2611.26828v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Delivering robust In-Building Coverage (IBC) is critically impeded by severe Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I) attenuation, a constraint that intensifies as deployments move from 5G mid-band towards mmWave and prospective 6G sub-THz carriers, where losses of 60-80 dB have been reported across modern building envelopes. While Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer scalable exterior RF sensing platforms, a fundamental inversion problem persists: interior 3D signal states cannot be directly sampled from constrained exterior flight paths. This paper proposes Graph-XGB, a hybrid inference framework that decouples spatial topology reasoning from non-linear signal regression to resolve this challenge. A modified SpiderGNN encoder, operating on a topology-aware graph constructed with a physically grounded Floor-Aware 3D Distance metric and Bridge Edge Guarantees, propagates UAV boundary measurements into 128-dimensional indoor embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) compresses these into a 10-dimensional manifold retaining 96.6% of embedding variance, fused with raw spatial features and decoded by independent, physics-tailored XGBoost regressors. This decoupling mitigates the optimization conflict between smoothly decaying path-loss signals and volatile interference-dependent metrics. Evaluated on a real-world 5G NR dataset of 613 verified nodes spanning the 10 floors of a single building, Graph-XGB attains the strongest accuracy among the architectures compared, with $R^2$ of 0.759 (RSSI) and 0.770 (RSRP), improvements of 35.5% and 64.9% over the SimpleGNN baseline, using no interior RF measurement as a model input; indoor observations enter only as training supervision, with evaluation on held-out internal nodes. Interference-dependent targets (RSRQ, SNR and CQI) remain bounded well below the path-loss metrics, delimiting the reach of purely spatial inference.
items.author: David Hason Rudd, Eunkwang Shin, Nithiwat Pattrapong, Huan Huo, Xiangmeng Wang
items.summary: Graph-XGB is a hybrid inference framework combining a modified SpiderGNN encoder for spatial topology reasoning with gradient-boosted regression to reconstruct indoor 3D 5G signal states from constrained exterior UAV flight paths, addressing the severe outdoor-to-indoor attenuation inversion problem.
items.reasoning: An applied domain-specific contribution combining established components (GNNs, XGBoost) for a concrete telecommunications problem. The engineering is reasonable and the application timely for mmWave deployment, but it is niche and methodologically incremental.

items.content_html: arXiv:2611.26828v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Delivering robust In-Building Coverage (IBC) is critically impeded by severe Outdoor-to-Indoor (O2I) attenuation, a constraint that intensifies as deployments move from 5G mid-band towards mmWave and prospective 6G sub-THz carriers, where losses of 60-80 dB have been reported across modern building envelopes. While Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) offer scalable exterior RF sensing platforms, a fundamental inversion problem persists: interior 3D signal states cannot be directly sampled from constrained exterior flight paths. This paper proposes Graph-XGB, a hybrid inference framework that decouples spatial topology reasoning from non-linear signal regression to resolve this challenge. A modified SpiderGNN encoder, operating on a topology-aware graph constructed with a physically grounded Floor-Aware 3D Distance metric and Bridge Edge Guarantees, propagates UAV boundary measurements into 128-dimensional indoor embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) compresses these into a 10-dimensional manifold retaining 96.6% of embedding variance, fused with raw spatial features and decoded by independent, physics-tailored XGBoost regressors. This decoupling mitigates the optimization conflict between smoothly decaying path-loss signals and volatile interference-dependent metrics. Evaluated on a real-world 5G NR dataset of 613 verified nodes spanning the 10 floors of a single building, Graph-XGB attains the strongest accuracy among the architectures compared, with $R^2$ of 0.759 (RSSI) and 0.770 (RSRP), improvements of 35.5% and 64.9% over the SimpleGNN baseline, using no interior RF measurement as a model input; indoor observations enter only as training supervision, with evaluation on held-out internal nodes. Interference-dependent targets (RSRQ, SNR and CQI) remain bounded well below the path-loss metrics, delimiting the reach of purely spatial inference.

items.title: Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction for Long-tailed Graph Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.27141v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Long-tailed graph classification (LTGC) is common in real-world graph datasets, where a few large head graphs provide rich structural information while many smaller tail graphs offer fewer structural cues, making it harder to learn discriminative representations for tail graphs. To address this size-based imbalance, we propose Dynamic Memory-enhanced Pattern Relevance Prediction (DMPRP), which transfers structural patterns from head graphs to tail graphs. Given a graph representation as a query, a dynamic expert memory module inspired by Knowledge-diverse Experts (KDEX) generates a residual vector that augments the original representation. We train the module using co-occurrence triplets sampled from head graphs at the node, rooted subgraph, and random-walk neighborhood levels. Experiments on five graph classification benchmarks show that DMPRP improves tail performance, and ablation studies show that both the expert module and random-walk supervision contribute to these gains. A controlled experiment on PTC further examines pattern transfer when smaller graphs are denser than larger ones. Our code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/DMPRP-73A5.

The module is trained with co-occurrence triplets sampled at node, rooted-subgraph, and graph levels.

items.title: To predict or to persist: how decoherence shapes learning in a spin-qubit quantum reservoir
items.content: arXiv:2611.26215v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In this work we investigate how dephasing and the choice of measured observables affect learning in a simulated six-qubit spin chain with Markovian dissipation and exact expectation-value readout. For externally driven nonlinear autoregressive moving-average signals, combining single- and two-qubit observables gives better predictions than a population-only readout at comparable polynomial feature counts. Most of the configurations we tested become more accurate than a reference with relaxation and dephasing disabled, most strongly at $T_2=1\,\mu$s, where total memory capacity drops, and still at $T_2=5$-$10\,\mu$s, where memory is only redistributed across delays. For autonomous generation, we train the readout with scheduled sampling and iterative dataset aggregation to expose it to states reached under its own feedback. We do not find a clear systematic dependence of limit-cycle persistence on coherence across the reservoir ensemble. For chaotic forecasting, in contrast, prediction horizons at $T_2=1\,\mu$s shorten in all 10 reservoir realizations relative to that reference. For the noise-driven strange non-chaotic attractor, the model produces a smooth, approximately closed orbit, and neither captures the target's scatter nor follows its trajectory pointwise. We conclude that, within this simulated reservoir, the impact of coherence depends strongly on the task.
items.author: Nikolaos Petropoulos, Elena Blokhina
items.summary: This simulation study of a six-qubit spin-chain quantum reservoir shows how dephasing and observable choice affect learning, finding that most configurations outperform a decoherence-free reference and that combined single- and two-qubit readouts beat population-only readout. It suggests decoherence can play a constructive role in quantum reservoir computing rather than being purely harmful.

items.title: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy: A judgment-aggregation perspective
items.content: arXiv:2611.27463v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Supervaluationism about vagueness and indeterminacy is based on the idea that some sentences, or predicates within them, have multiple competing interpretations or specifications. A sentence is deemed determinately true if and only if it is true according to all specifications; and determinately false if and only if it is false according to all specifications. In all other cases, the sentence is assigned no determinate truth-value. Supervaluationism, however, is only one way of taking into account the verdicts of different specifications -- in technical terms, "aggregating" those verdicts. In this paper, we introduce insights from the theory of judgment aggregation to study a broad class of different aggregation functions. This allows us to offer an axiomatic characterization of supervaluationism, which, in turn, locates it precisely within a larger logical space of possible approaches to vagueness and indeterminacy. Among other results, we axiomatically compare supervaluationism with subvaluationism, the epistemic theory of vagueness, and Strong Kleene and LP logics.
items.author: Christian List, Paul Egr\'e, Franz Dietrich
items.summary: This theory paper reframes supervaluationism about vagueness through the lens of judgment aggregation, treating the truth verdicts of competing specifications as objects of aggregation. It studies a broad class of aggregation functions beyond the universal-agreement rule supervaluationism implicitly uses.
items.reasoning: Rigorous and conceptually interesting formal philosophy with potential relevance to handling vagueness in AI reasoning, but it is foundational theory with no direct empirical AI application demonstrated.

items.title: Learning 3D MRI Representations with Generative Adversarial Networks
items.content: arXiv:2611.27057v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Learning representations of visual images is a challenging task. It requires extracting abstract patterns from high-dimensional data without explicit supervision. This becomes pronounced with 3D MR imaging due to sparse features, higher dimensional inputs, and smaller datasets. Many state-of-the-art representation learning algorithms successfully rely on transformers and diffusion-based architectures. However, these methods struggle with smaller datasets. In effect, solution methods relax the problem by slicing 3D volumes and solving the problem for 2D medical imaging, resulting in a loss of spatial 3D information. We present R2RG, a representation learning method based on Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) honing the reconstruction task. Our key insights lie in exploiting architectural biases in 3D CNNs, combined with data-efficient auto-encoding GANs and a composite loss function to enhance reconstruction fidelity and stabilize training. Our experiments on three standard datasets and a locally collected dataset show that R2RG not only achieves superior performance but also generalizes to heterogeneous and smaller datasets. Furthermore, representations learned with R2RG outperform those learned with contrastive-based representation learning methods on Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease classification. Our work demonstrates that reconstruction-based representation learning is a promising direction for 3D medical imaging under limited data availability.
items.author: Sujeet Lahane, Sapna Mishra, Akash Suryavanshi, Tapan Gandhi, Bharat Biswal
items.summary: R2RG is a CNN-and-GAN based representation learning method for full 3D MRI volumes, motivated by the observation that transformer and diffusion approaches struggle with small medical datasets and that 2D slicing loses spatial information. It targets label-free extraction of abstract patterns from high-dimensional 3D medical imaging.

items.title: Can Reasoning and Image Description Enhance Yes/No Visual Mathematical Understanding?
items.content: arXiv:2611.27302v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have achieved strong performance on general visual tasks, yet their ability to understand mathematical images remains limited. This paper investigates whether explicit reasoning and textual image descriptions can enhance VLMs' performance on binary yes/no visual mathematical questions. To achieve this, we curated a paired evaluation set to benchmark prominent open-source VLMs under varying prompt and input conditions. In particular, we leverage Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and use textual descriptions, either replacing or augmenting visual inputs, to isolate and evaluate mathematical comprehension. Our results show that explicit reasoning improves performance, especially in paired consistency accuracy, while textual image descriptions do not consistently help and may degrade performance. These findings suggest that reasoning is important for stable visual mathematical judgement, whereas description-based intermediates require more careful design.

items.title: Quantitative Measurement of Pavement Distress based on Vehicle Camera and Perspective Correction
items.content: arXiv:2611.27728v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Using image data is becoming an important method for highway agencies to automatically evaluate pavement conditions. However, most studies focus on improving detection accuracy rather than obtaining quantitative measurements, such as the length or area of pavement distress. Although field camera calibration can provide such measurements, it is impractical for large volumes of onboard images collected from different vehicles. This study develops a method to quantitatively measure pavement distress directly from in-vehicle camera images without on-site camera calibration. A quadrilateral region of interest is first identified based on lane detection and used to construct a perspective transformation matrix for image correction. Size correction is then performed using the proportions of road markings in the image and a specified scale, which also enables estimation of the actual width of the selected region. The corrected images are subsequently processed using object detection algorithms to obtain quantitative distress measurements. The proposed method can efficiently perform perspective correction for images collected by the same vehicle camera with minimal manual effort. The measured pavement patch lengths show a trend consistent with pavement friction data. By calibrating vehicle cameras using only image information, this study enables quantitative pavement distress detection without additional field experiments. The approach provides a practical solution for processing large volumes of vehicle-camera data, particularly as connected vehicles generate increasing amounts of uncalibrated roadway imagery.

items.title: NitroGen: Observations on the Action Dynamics, Visual Instruction Following, and Spatial Exploration
items.content: arXiv:2611.26807v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: NitroGen is an open vision-action foundation model for game control. It is trained by behavior cloning on online gameplay videos. In this paper, we study the frozen controller in Hollow Knight and Trackmania as examples along three dimensions: action adaptation, visual instruction following, and spatial exploration. Our results indicate that NitroGen can adapt its actions to local context, but it lacks the planning, recovery, and exploration needed for longer-horizon game control.

items.title: Online Learning for Minimizing Maximum Tardiness in Single-Machine Scheduling
items.content: arXiv:2611.27067v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We study online learning for minimizing maximum tardiness (\OMMT) in single-machine scheduling. In each round, the learner selects a permutation of \(n\) fixed jobs, representing a schedule. The environment then reveals a processing time and a due date for each job, and the learner incurs a vector-valued loss whose components correspond to the tardiness of the individual jobs. The goal of the learner is to minimize \(\alpha\)-regret, the difference between the learner's maximum cumulative tardiness and \(\alpha\) times that of the best fixed permutation in hindsight, for as small \(\alpha\) as possible. We investigate OMMT under both stochastic and adversarial environments. In the stochastic setting, we prove that the expected \(1\)-regret of the Follow-the-Leader (FTL) algorithm is \(   O\!\left(\frac{n\log n}{\Delta^2}\right) \), together with a corresponding high-probability bound, where \(\Delta\) is a distribution-dependent gap parameter. At round \(t \in \{1,\dots,T\}\), FTL runs in \(O(tn^2)\) time and \(O(tn)\) space. In the adversarial setting, we prove that, for any \(0<\log_2 n/16\), the \(\alpha\)-regret is \(\Omega(T)\) whenever \(\alpha<\log_2 n/16-c\). We then reduce OMMT to a surrogate online learning problem and apply Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader (FTPL), obtaining an expected \(\alpha\)-regret bound of \(O(n^2\sqrt{T})\) for \(\alpha=O(\log n)\). Thus, the logarithmic dependence of \(\alpha\) on \(n\) is tight up to constant factors. Each FTPL update admits a mixed-integer programming formulation whose size is polynomial in \(n\) and \(t\).

items.summary: This paper formulates an online learning problem where a learner repeatedly selects permutations of fixed jobs for single-machine scheduling, incurring vector-valued tardiness losses, with the goal of minimizing alpha-regret against the best fixed schedule. The authors derive regret bounds for both stochastic and adversarial environments.
items.reasoning: Solid theoretical work bridging online learning and scheduling theory with regret guarantees, but a specialized combinatorial setting with limited direct relevance to broader ML practice.

items.title: Quantum-Informed Regularized Poisson Learning for Graph-Based Semi-Supervised Classification
items.content: arXiv:2611.27609v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: We introduce IPQSSL, a quantum-informed regularized Poisson framework for graph-based semi-supervised classification under scarce labels. Local graph feature contexts are QR factorized, lifted to unitary encodings, and processed by a shared variational circuit whose measurements yield node wise diagonal weights that stabilize a symmetrized Poisson system. We establish positive definiteness of the symmetrized, regularized operator under explicit spectral conditions and derive a Hermitian, block encoding compatible formulation that separates the classical NISQ oriented implementation from a future fault-tolerant pathway. Across seven benchmarks spanning tabular data and a citation network, the effect of regularization is dataset- and budget-dependent: IPQSSL improves over the Poisson baselines on Iris and Wine at all but the single-label budget, reaching 0.946 accuracy on Iris at ten labels per class and at every budget on German Credit, where, however, all methods remain below the majority class rate. Original Poisson remains preferable on Breast Cancer, Heart Disease, Optdigits, and Cora, with the deficit narrowing as the label budget grows on the two largest graphs. Ablations attribute the gains to diagonal stabilization rather than variational training. The result is a resource transparent bridge between Poisson graph learning and quantum linear algebra, with an explicit empirical delineation of when diagonal regularization helps.

items.title: On the Complete Feature Set for ADHD Classification in Children and Adolescents Based on EEG Signals
items.content: arXiv:2611.27970v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.

items.summary: The authors curate 669 BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions into a standardized resource linking continuous EEG to 115 precomputed feature definitions, with documented quality decisions and consistent analysis windows.
