items.content_html: arXiv:2611.27970v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is a neurodevelopmental condition that can affect attention, activity and impulse control. Electroencephalography (EEG) records brain activity as children and adolescents perform cognitive tasks. However, comparing features derived from these recordings requires consistent signal preparation, shared analysis windows and documented quality decisions. We curated 669 existing BALLADEER recordings from 156 participants across five task conditions so that researchers can compare seven EEG feature families on the same time intervals for each participant and task. The dataset links continuous signals to precomputed measurements from 115 feature definitions or templates and records the quality decisions made for each recording. Analyses must still account for repeated measurements within participants, residual artefacts and differences between acquisition systems. Technical validation covered signal integrity, numerical checks on feature estimators and completeness of the released files. In every task, the median proportion of recording time retained after preprocessing was 100%. To illustrate reuse, we report saved participant-held-out evaluations comparing XGBoost using all seven families on eight-second windows with a predictor based only on recruitment-group prevalence in the training fold. Recruitment-group discrimination was stronger in Robots than in the three Slackline conditions. These descriptive results from overlapping cohorts do not establish diagnostic validity. The dataset, curation software and aggregate results for the predictive example are publicly available.

items.title: CanopyFormer: Attention-Guided SegFormer for Explainable Forest Cover Segmentation
items.content: arXiv:2611.27674v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: In transformer segmentation models, attention is usually visualized after training rather than supervised. Although attention supervision has been explored for natural images and driving scenes, aerial forest segmentation typically uses attention only as an architectural component and evaluates interpretability qualitatively. We present CanopyFormer, an attention-guided SegFormer-B0 that uses an Attention Consistency Loss to align attention with the ground-truth forest mask, encouraging attention to focus on canopy regions. Since SegFormer uses spatial-reduction attention, we adapt Gradient-weighted Attention Rollout by restricting it to the final encoder stage, where the attention matrix is square. We introduce Average Attention-Mask Overlap (AAMO) to measure attention alignment and incorporate a deletion test to evaluate faithfulness. On 5108 images, our method increases AAMO from 0.0334 to 0.7476, approximately 22 times the vanilla SegFormer-B0 result, with a modest decrease in Dice score from 0.8743 to 0.8577. The deletion test reveals that improved alignment does not necessarily translate into improved faithfulness: removing the most-attended 25% of patches reduces the forest score by 12.1%, compared with 33.0% when removing random patches. Attention supervision introduces no additional inference cost, although double backpropagation makes each training step 2.6 to 2.8 times slower. The attention alignment improvement also generalizes to a second dataset, LoveDA. Additionally, a Boundary Refinement Module provides no consistent Dice improvement and reduces AAMO, while mean squared error substantially outperforms Kullback-Leibler divergence as the attention loss.
items.author: Dhinanjaya Fernando, Dinura Ginige, Kalana Lakshan, Chanupa Gurusinghe, Lasana Pahanga, Dileesha Manamperi, Thimira Sahan, Sandareka Wickramanayake
items.summary: Presents CanopyFormer, a SegFormer-B0 variant with an Attention Consistency Loss that supervises attention maps against ground-truth forest masks for aerial forest segmentation. items.reasoning: Reasonable applied contribution combining attention supervision with explainability in a niche domain, but the method is an incremental modification of an existing architecture and evaluation is likely limited in scale.

items.title: Automating Multi-View Quality Assessment of 3D Annotation Layouts
items.content: arXiv:2611.27621v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Text labels provide descriptive information about elements in visual scenes. In 3D visualization, the arrangement of these labels and their connections to target locations forms an annotation layout. Assessing layout quality supports comparisons between alternative layouts. However, existing quality measures often focus on specific layout properties and may not fully reflect human judgments of overall quality. Moreover, a layout may appear clear from one viewpoint but suffer from occlusion or clutter from another. To address these issues, we propose a multi-view quality assessment method based on a multimodal large language model (MLLM). We fine-tune a compact MLLM using structured supervision from human ratings to predict a rating for each quality dimension in each view. These ratings are aggregated into view-level and sample-level quality scores. To support training and evaluation, we construct the Annotation Layouts with Quality Assessment (ALQA) dataset, containing 3,216 layout samples from 1,072 3D objects across 13 categories. Each layout is rendered from 5 predefined viewpoints, and each view is independently rated by 3 human raters across 5 quality dimensions. On ALQA, our method agrees more closely with human reference scores than the evaluated MLLM baselines, and a user study demonstrates strong agreement with human preferences in layout ranking.

items.title: Frontier Voltage Boost Laplacian Path Planning
items.content: arXiv:2611.27308v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: This paper introduces Frontier Voltage Boost Laplacian path planning. The method inherits many of the attractive features of earlier Harmonic Potential Field planning methods, including absence of local minima and smooth paths, while improving the original. The piecewise approach we introduce is able to solve larger maps and handle narrow passages more quickly than earlier Harmonic Potential Field methods. After explaining the algorithm, we experimentally characterize its cor- rectness, performance, and path smoothness as a function of map size. Code is available at https://github.com/vpritamani/FrontierVoltageBoostLaplacianPathPlanning
items.author: Vinay Pritamani, Rishabh Jain, Jack Lowry, Joshua Smith
items.summary: This paper improves Harmonic Potential Field path planning with a piecewise frontier voltage boost method that retains freedom from local minima and path smoothness while handling larger maps and narrow passages faster. The algorithm is characterized experimentally for correctness, performance, and smoothness, with code released. It is a focused refinement of classical potential-field planning.
items.reasoning: A competent but narrow classical-planning refinement with limited connection to current learning-based robotics trends; usefulness is real for certain applications, but novelty and broader impact are modest.

items.title: Can Language Models See the Circuit in Pixelated RFIC Passives?
items.content: arXiv:2611.27559v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: The emergence of inverse-designed, pixelated passives for microwave and millimeter-wave applications has been a major development in the field of RFIC design. These devices, which appear to be QR-code-like in structure, exist in a generalizable, high-dimensional design space that includes conventional passive topologies. However, these structures are naturally unintuitive for designers, and failures or deviations in performance are difficult to debug. In this work, we ask whether a frontier language model can understand, predict, and edit the responses and layout structure of pixelated passives. The agent, run with all tools disabled, is first asked to read layouts on 18x18 and 27x27 tile grids and, in a single reply, predict the input impedance and loss of the structure from 20-100 GHz. On eight GA-synthesized layouts and five random fills, the predicted Smith-chart locus follows full-wave simulation results closely, with a systematic shift that places features about 16% lower in frequency than EM. On multipath loop structures it identifies notches successfully but shows a smaller frequency bias, about half that of an ideal transmission-line model that ignores bends. The agent is then asked to debug seven designs that fail their specification, and given a budget of five EM simulations and at most twelve changed tiles, it is able to improve all seven and bring five designs within specification. These experiments suggest language models can serve as an interpretability and debugging tool for traditionally non-intuitive inverse-designed passives.

items.reasoning: An intriguing cross-domain capability probe of frontier models in an unusual engineering domain, but it is an exploratory evaluation with unclear broader methodology or transferable findings.

items.title: Parameter-Efficient Adaptation of Qwen3-VL for Handwritten Mathematical Expression Recognition
items.content: arXiv:2611.27208v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Handwritten mathematical expression recognition (HMER) requires joint recovery of symbol identity and two-dimensional syntax, so a locally plausible transcription may still be structurally wrong. We study whether a compact vision-language model can be adapted to generate linearized Symbol Label Graphs (SLGs) under limited computing resources. Starting from a 4-bit Qwen3-VL-4B checkpoint, we apply rank-16 Low-Rank Adaptation to the vision, language, attention, and MLP modules and train with instruction-formatted CROHME 2019 examples. We compare this model with an internally implemented ViT-Transformer baseline, a zero-shot Qwen3-VL configuration, and additional internally evaluated alternatives. On the 1,198 valid CROHME test examples, the CROHME-only model obtains 524 exact matches (43.74%) and a corpus BLEU-4 score of 77.67, compared with 4.92% and 43.26 for the task-specific ViT baseline. An ablation that adds 2,000 manually written, formula-guided samples decreases exact match to 42.32%, exposing a domain-alignment issue rather than an automatic benefit from more data. The principal contribution is therefore an evidence-backed, resource-efficient formulation of HMER as multimodal structural generation, together with a controlled data-composition ablation and an analysis of the remaining gap between local token overlap and globally correct structure.
items.author: Manh Tuan Ha, Xuan Bao Viet Tran, Vo Minh Dat Nguyen, Minh Nhat Vo, Quoc Trung Nguyen, Van Bay Nguyen

It explores whether compact VLMs can capture two-dimensional mathematical syntax under limited compute.

items.title: BioCL-POS: Biological Completer-aware Learning with Predictive Observation Selection - A Wild Ginseng Study
items.content: arXiv:2611.27316v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Growers and traders rely on root morphology to assess wild ginseng, yet breakage can obscure important structural traits. We study point cloud completion to provide geometric references for morphological analysis. Does providing more observed points always improve 3D completion? We test whether selected subsets improve recovery of the original missing region while keeping the pretrained completer fixed. We introduce BioCL-POS, an external selector that predicts how the completer responds to candidate inputs. For each candidate, we predict the displacement and distance from shared spatial locations to the nearest points in its completion. We use these spatial responses to estimate recovery quality and supervise them with measurements from actual completions. At inference, we select an input from the observed geometry and run the completer once. We evaluate four frozen completers on controlled gaps in ginseng and tree data at 5%,10%, and 20% omission, and examine 30% omission on ginseng. At 5--20% omission, we outperform full-input completion and all five alternative selectors on both datasets with all four completers. We achieve lower mean reconstruction error and higher mean F-score and coverage. We thus show that selecting observations can improve geometric recovery without retraining the completer, providing more accurate geometric references for subsequent morphological analysis.

items.reasoning: An interesting niche application combining completer-aware observation selection with a specific agricultural use case, but the narrow domain and incremental methodological contribution limit broader impact.

items.title: A Switching Mechanism for Selecting Environment-Adaptive Personalized Gains in Hearing Aids
items.content: arXiv:2611.27726v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Personalized amplification gains for hearing aids have been shown to be preferred over prescriptive gains. Since the preferred settings can vary depending on the background audio environment, this paper presents a switching mechanism or system that automatically selects personalized gains for a current background audio environment. To prevent foreground speech from interfering with background environment analysis, a one-class voice activity detector is designed to identify speech activity from speech mixed with noise. A consistency check is conducted to enable distinguishing foreground speech from background speech, preserving babble as a background environment of interest because hearing aid users often struggle to understand speech in background babble. Sound segments without foreground speech are then analyzed by an online discovery method combining Bayesian change-point detection with a memory of previously encountered environments. This discovery method detects changes, recognizes returning environments, and discovers new ones without a predefined number of environments. Experimental results show that three-seed mean macro-averaged F1 scores of 85.53%-91.98% across eight speech/background-corpus pairs covering 36 background noise types were achieved. Furthermore, the discovery method achieved adjusted Rand indices of 0.91 and 0.96 on two families of test streams. In the same-recording-return condition of audio streams combining speech with four background audio environments often encountered by hearing aid users, the switching mechanism selected the correct personalized gain profile after 105 environment changes, recalled the stored gain profile at every return, and made no switches to an incorrect gain profile.

items.reasoning: Practical, well-motivated signal-processing and ML application with clear accessibility impact, but narrow scope and incremental methodological novelty relative to core ML research.

items.title: A Unified Framework for Intelligent Cyber Attack Detection and Alert Correlation
items.content: arXiv:2611.26824v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: A Security Operations Center (SOC) plays a critical role in detecting, correlating, and responding to modern cyber threats. However, SOCs continue to face challenges related to alert overload, fragmented detection capabilities, and limited collaboration between analysts and automated systems. These issues often result in delayed incident response, analyst fatigue, and an increased risk of overlooking sophisticated, multi-stage attacks that unfold gradually across different layers of the network. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a unified framework for network traffic classification and alert correlation through the use of signature rules, machine learning, and sequential pattern mining algorithms. The solution was evaluated in a controlled testbed environment emulating realistic, multi-stage attack scenarios, including malware exploitation, lateral movement, reconnaissance, and data exfiltration. The obtained results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in detecting and correlating complex attack behaviors, while providing analysts with actionable insights in line with a human-in-the-loop approach to SOC operations.

It was evaluated to show improved coordination between analysts and automated detection.
items.reasoning: Relevant applied cybersecurity contribution addressing genuine SOC pain points, but the approach integrates established techniques rather than introducing new ML methodology.

items.title: Cross-Linguistic Distinctive-Feature Constraints on Segmental Triphones: Evidence for Contrastive Dispersion
items.content: arXiv:2611.26837v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Natural speech reflects articulatory and perceptual constraints, yet how these pressures shape consecutive segment transitions across languages remains underexplored. We analyze adjacent distinctive-feature distances in token-weighted segmental triphones across 17 Universal Dependencies corpora spanning nine language families, transcribed into IPA and mapped to 24 PanPhon features using Hamming and cosine metrics. Natural sequences exhibit an intermediate-distance mode (8-10 features under Hamming, except Vietnamese; 0.28-0.38 under cosine). Against an unrestricted within-word shuffled baseline, natural words reject the inventory-only null (W = 0, p < 10-4), showing higher expected distance, narrower dispersion, and lower joint triphone entropy in all 17 languages. Under a stricter within-word consonant-vowel template baseline, expected distance and dispersion are no longer separated, whereas joint entropy remains lower in 16 languages (p = 1.07x10-4). Entropy decomposition reveals higher mutual information between incoming and outgoing transitions in all 17 languages and all nine families (W = 0, p < 10-4), demonstrating sequential coupling beyond syllable-template alternation. Word-level mean-SD correlations and directional asymmetries do not replicate cross-linguistically.

items.reasoning: Careful cross-linguistic empirical analysis with solid statistics, contributing to computational phonology and typology, but of niche relevance to the broader machine learning community.

items.title: Adesktop learning factory for smart and resilient manufacturing based on digital twin and AI
items.content: arXiv:2611.27579v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Learning factories have been increasingly applied in engineering research and education. In this paper, we develop a small-scale, low-cost, fully open-sourced learning factory that leverages AI and digital twins to demonstrate smart and resilient manufacturing. The learning factory consists of an AGV, three robots, two conveyors and their digital twins. Three typical use cases are designed to demonstrate the capabilities of the learning factory, i.e., material sorting through computer vision-based robot control, coordinating AGV, robots and conveyors for assembly, and digital twin-driven predictive maintenance. The results show that the developed learning factory can adequately support the teaching and research activities on digital twins and AI on manufacturing. Its fully open-source architecture and relatively low deployment cost make it an ideal solution for universities and research institutions.

items.title: Condensation: Motivation and Definitions
items.content:
Thanks to Santiago Cifuentes for reading and commenting on the draft.

# Introduction

Sam Eisenstat’s paper on Condensation is very cool, but I found it pretty hard-going to read. There are already several nice explainers (Abram Demski's two posts, Daniel and Jeremy's post on Condensation and Natural Latents and Jan's Elementary Condensation). This post and its sequel will be a little different in that, the main substance (after the introductory sections) will be 'close readings' of the mathematical content of the paper, picking through important definitions and theorems, explaining them, giving some intuitions and going through examples. I find doing this kind of thing helpful when I'm trying to understand a new idea. I'll try to be fairly mathematically rigourous, yet much less formal than the paper. Whenever I give a definition or theorem, I'll try to add a note in brackets detailing the corresponding section in the paper.

I have spoken to several people who said that they found reading the paper hard. As a result, I have erred on the side of over-explaining rather than under-explaining, including examples rather than assuming they're obvious and repeating myself rather than assuming I was understood the first time I stated something. Because of this, this has ended up being pretty long and I have split it up into two (possibly more) posts. This first post contains:

- An intuitive motivation for condensation and why we might care about this for the purpose of AI safety.
- Definitions and examples of Random Variable Models and Latent Variable Models.
- Explanations of the scoring functions and some proofs of their properties

This post doesn't contain any of the main theorems, but the next post will contain proofs of the perfect condensation theorems. These will be much easier to state and prove once we have established the machinery and motivation in this post.

items.title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence with Learning Style Models: Opportunities, Challenges, and Future Directions
items.content: arXiv:2611.27868v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) has emerged as a powerful tool for transforming learning. This review examines how Generative AI can be integrated with established learning style models (VARK, Kolb, Felder-Silverman, and Honey & Mumford) to support student engagement in large online classes. Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, we searched Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar (2015 to 2026) and included 41 studies that met the eligibility criteria. The review maps Generative AI capabilities to learning style preferences, synthesizes existing implementations, highlights benefits and challenges, and proposes pathways for future research and practice. Despite ongoing debates regarding the empirical validity of learning styles, Generative AI enables flexible, multimodal, and real-time adaptation. This study offers practical insights for educators and developers seeking to build more effective, learner centered learning systems

It synthesizes implementations, benefits, and challenges, while acknowledging ongoing debates about the empirical validity of learning styles.

items.title: Neural Defend Ranks #1 in Global Audio Deepfake Detection Benchmark - ARCAS on the Podonos Independent Leaderboard
items.content: arXiv:2611.27215v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Commercial detectors of AI-generated audio are usually promoted with results on internal test sets that buyers cannot inspect. Independent benchmarks with private labels give a more reliable comparison. We report the results of Neural Defend's ARCAS foundation models on the Podonos audio deepfake detection benchmark, an independent leaderboard that scores commercial detection APIs and open-source detectors on one held-out set of real speech and speech from current text-to-speech and voice-cloning systems, delivered in six file formats, against labels that only Podonos holds. In the release of 29 October 2026, which covers 28 systems from 16 commercial vendors and the leading open models, ARCAS 290M and the smaller ARCAS 90M share first place, ahead of every other commercial system, including Resemble AI, Hiya, Pindrop, Hive, and Reality Defender. Both models make fewer errors than any other system by a statistically clear margin, keep false positives and false negatives in balance at their default threshold, process every submitted file without rejection, and sit on the accuracy--latency frontier of the leaderboard. As for every commercial system added since Podonos retired its API runner, the ARCAS predictions were submitted by Neural Defend and scored by Podonos against its private labels. We describe the benchmark's construction and protocol in full, reproduce the complete leaderboard and its history across five releases, and analyse error balance, statistical separation, speed, and the gap between commercial and open-source detectors. The results agree with the companion evaluation of ARCAS 290M on the complete test sets of ten public benchmarks and establish ARCAS as the most accurate AI-generated audio detector evaluated on this independent benchmark.

items.title: Ranking-Preserving Coreset Selection for Efficient Evolutionary Hyperparameter Optimization
items.content: arXiv:2611.27959v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Hyperparameter optimization (HPO) is essential for high predictive performance, but its computational cost becomes prohibitive when candidate configurations require repeated training on large datasets. This paper proposes a ranking-preserving coreset (RPC) selection framework for accelerating evolutionary HPO. The method constructs a compact coreset that preserves the relative ranking of hyperparameter configurations observed on the full training data. Coreset selection is formulated as an evolutionary optimization problem that maximizes Spearman rank correlation between full-data and subset-based configuration rankings while penalizing subset size. The selected coreset is then used for HPO with three evolutionary algorithms: Genetic Algorithm (GA), Cross-generational elitist Selection, Heterogeneous Recombination and Cataclysmic Mutation (CHC), and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO). Experiments on seven tabular, two text, and two image benchmark datasets show that RPC substantially reduces HPO time while maintaining test accuracy comparable to full-dataset HPO across decision tree, text classification, and image classification tasks. Across datasets and optimizers, HPO-stage speedups range from approximately 1.14x to 8.80x, while the one-time coreset construction cost is accounted for separately through end-to-end runtime and break-even analysis. On 20 held-out configurations excluded from coreset construction, RPC achieves higher ranking correlation than same-size random sampling on 8 of 11 datasets (dataset-level Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p = 0.014). These results show that ranking preservation extends beyond the configurations used during selection. The one-time construction cost can be amortized when the coreset is reused across HPO runs.

items.title: Obstacles to mindreading: Simple, irreducible, and instrumental opacity
items.content:
Sometimes there's an entity in the world, and after observing that entity's behavior, I choose to model it as an agent: that is, something that "seeks" some objective. I think I usually do this because I want to predict the entity's behavior in circumstances I haven't observed.

- I see a weird, wet-looking thing on a rock, moving slowly, with a trail of slime behind it. I might choose to model it as seeking to move in some particular direction. I avoid putting my book down right in front of it, to avoid getting slug slime on my book.
- I see a tree growing in a cave, with all its branches growing toward the cave entrance. I might choose to model it as aiming for its leaves to be in the sunlight. After seeing lots of examples I might generalize: trees aim for their leaves to be in the sun - I might arrange my garden so that the effect of the trees seeking sunlight is visually pleasing, and the trees' growth toward sunlight won't block pathways in the garden.
- I see a man with half a plate of food in front of him, fork moving some of the food into his mouth, seeming to enjoy the meal. I might choose to model him as seeking to ingest the food. "I'll have what he's having," I tell the waiter.

"Why is it doing that?" I might ask, about an entity. Some answers will be "internal" reasons (internal to the frame of treating that entity as an agent).

- "He answered 'A' for that question because he believes Napoleon was German"
- "It grabbed the fruit because it's hungry"

Other answers will be "external" reasons, that don't stay inside the agentic frame.

- "It's moving its legs like that because its neurons are firing in such-and-such a pattern and that's leading its muscles to contract like so"
- "It's falling because it is denser than the medium it's embedded in"

Often, internal reasons have internal reasons of their own....
items.author: benwr
items.summary: This essay develops a taxonomy of obstacles to understanding other agents' goals and internals, distinguishing simple, irreducible, and instrumental forms of opacity through everyday examples like slugs, trees, and diners. It grounds agent-modeling and mindreading difficulties in intuition-pumping cases relevant to how humans might understand AI systems.
items.reasoning: A careful conceptual piece with relevance to interpretability and agent modeling, particularly the instrumental opacity notion that agents may have incentives to resist being modeled. It lacks formal results or empirical work, but the taxonomy could sharpen discussions of AI opacity and monitoring.

items.title: Comparative Performance of Machine Learning Architectures for Fault Detection and Diagnosis in Chemical Processes
items.content: arXiv:2611.27696v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Fault Detection and Diagnosis (FDD) is crucial for both maintenance and control in chemical industries, where early fault detection can prevent costly failures and optimize operations. This is particularly critical in pilot units like those at IFP Energies Nouvelles (IFPEN), which operate under short-term experimental conditions with frequently varying operational parameters. This study conducts an extensive benchmarking analysis using the Tennessee Eastman Process (TEP), a widely used simulated chemical process dataset, to evaluate multiple approaches for fault detection and diagnosis, featuring numerous continuous operations with different sensors and faults. Several methods were implemented and compared including Multi Scale PCA (MS-PCA), AutoEncoder, Ensemble Learning, and LSTM models for fault detection, alongside Random Forest, XGBoost, and BLSTM (Bidirectional LSTM) for fault diagnosis. Our results demonstrate that Ensemble Learning achieves detection rates ranging from 80% to 100% across various fault scenarios. For the fault diagnosis task, BLSTM achieved a diagnosis accuracy of 98.76%. The study reveals that ensemble-based approaches consistently outperform individual models in handling the complex, multivariate nature of chemical process data, due to its robustness in combining multiple perspectives, comprehensive data capture, and localized detection capabilities. Furthermore, the superior performance of the BLSTM is due to its ability to capture both past and future temporal dependencies in the sequential data, particularly important in chemical processes where fault patterns may manifest with complex temporal relationships. This research contributes to the field of Fault Detection and Diagnosis by providing empirical evidence for the effectiveness of ensemble methods and Bidirectional LSTMs in order to address industrial FDD applications on chemical processes.

items.title: Piercing My Ear for the Whispering Earring
items.content:
Fourteen years ago, Scott Alexander wrote of the
Whispering
Earring.  It's a

cautionary tale of an earring that advises you,
and to which you increasingly defer as you realize its suggestions are
better than you'd do otherwise.  You become very
successful, but in the end there's nothing of you left.  Ten days
after Scott published the story, AlexNet won ImageNet 2012 by a huge
margin, kicking off the deep learning revolution.

The earring whispers advice as "better for you if you...", and it's
always right. While AI today would have seemed like distant science
fiction in 2012, it's still far from infallible.  I expect AI to
continue getting better quickly, but don't expect it ever gets to
"always right".  A Whispering Earring dynamic with AI, however,
doesn't need infallibility.  Instead, like playing Go with AlphaGo in
your ear, the AI just needs to be capable enough that you can't
improve on its advice. [1]

That's not where we are today.  I use AI heavily, both in my
professional and personal life, but we're working together.  The AI
makes mistakes and I catch them; I make mistakes and the AI catches
them.  It does much more of the work, but overall it's a
brilliant—if uneven—collaborator.

I like this stage a lot, but it's clear it's not stopping
here.  AI is now speeding
up the process of making AI (and I think we should
slow down).  But even without much recursive self-improvement,
Fable 5.2 needs me much less than Opus 5.5, which already needed me
much less than Opus 4.5 did.  A year ago collaboration was like
working with a very fast junior staff member who could take a
well-scoped problem and provide something I needed to check carefully.
Today the best models still do dumb things, but probably less often
than I do....
items.author: jefftk
items.summary: The author connects Scott Alexander's 2012 Whispering Earring parable to current AI assistance, arguing that AI does not need to be infallible to create a deference dynamic, only capable enough that users cannot improve on its advice. The essay contrasts today's collaborative human-AI working relationships with an anticipated future of unilateral deference, framed by the author's decision to get an earring.
items.reasoning: A well-written meditation on AI-assisted decision-making and gradual deference dynamics that echoes real concerns about cognitive offloading and value drift. It is personal commentary without empirical content, but the threshold framing of deference (infallibility not required) is a genuinely useful intuition.

items.title: How Much of a Calculation-Error Rate Is Not Arithmetic: Auditing the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 Metric with a Deterministic Rule System
items.content: arXiv:2611.27192v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic.   The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.
items.author: Vladimir Beskorovainyi
items.summary: Audits the FinReason Cup 2026 Task 3 metric and shows its calculation-error label does not actually count arithmetic failures, since one rule yields answers that are negations of reported values across all practice cases. items.content_html: arXiv:2611.27192v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Task 3 of the FinReason Cup 2026 scores a system on two values per case, the one an XBRL filing reports and the one its own calculation relationships imply, and labels each failure as structural, extraction or calculation. This report shows that the calculation-error rate so defined does not count arithmetic failures, and bounds how far it is from one using the published board alone. One of the three rules behind the benchmark, DQC_US_0015, has an answer that is the negation of the reported value (in all 110 published practice cases, against 1 of 120 and 6 of 102 for the other two), so a calculation label on such a case records a wrong fact or a wrong route, not a wrong sum. Subtracting the available structural and extraction labels from each entry's error count on that rule gives a floor: the bound is positive for 22 of the 23 ranked entries, and at the top it is sharpest, with at least 11 of 12 and 12 of 13 calculation errors of the two joint-first entries falling on cases where no arithmetic remained. The calculation-error rate of the best systems on this task is almost entirely not arithmetic. The vehicle for that result is an entry that reconstructs the three data-quality rules the benchmark is drawn from, DQC_US_0015, DQC_US_0117 and DQC_US_0126, as a deterministic system with no learned parameters, no training step and no external service, running all 680 cases in 1.4 seconds. It scores 96.62% under the offline judge on development and 95.29% on the published test set, and its residual error concentrates in cases where a concept carries several equally flagged facts and the question names no dimensional member. Reading those error classes against the per-rule accuracies is what exposed the metric, which is why both are reported here.

items.title: Do we know what we are building?
items.content:
Late at night, almost half asleep, I went to pick up the packages from the mailroom and out of nowhere I found myself chatting about AI with the doorman while he was handing me the packages. He started showing me the apps and gaming websites he’s been building with coding agents, including a secure app that summarizes pretty much all the activities happening behind the scenes - who posted what, who DM’ed, emails, all account activities on your phone, since you last checked, all in a single app. Pretty impressive, right? At least that’s what I thought on my way back.

My first question to him was “how much do you understand what you are building? Are you a coder?” to which he replied “No - I am not!”. Immediately in my head I was like “Maybe I shouldn’t have asked that”. Seeing your ideas come to life is empowering and satisfying, in a way I undermined that by questioning his credentials.

Not having an expensive degree has never stopped anyone from creating something they believed in. They would go on their journey of self-studying, learning whatever was necessary, or finding people who knew how to build products. But in today’s Agentic age, what’s the point of the grind? Use Claude Code or Codex - you can have your ideas built in hours, or days at most. Why waste your time studying or understanding how the code underlying your products really works?

Ideas are cheap now, but understanding what you build is very expensive....

items.title: NightmareDiscourseBench: A Benchmark Dataset for Fictional Direct Discourse Identification Pipelines
items.content: arXiv:2611.27059v1 Announce Type: new  Abstract: In this paper we introduce a new benchmark dataset, NightmareDiscourseBench, for testing NLP pipelines that identify forms of direct discourse in English-language fiction. We first review existing publicly available benchmarks (providing summary statistics and reviewing available metadata) for this task, identifying theoretical inconsistency and exclusive focus on speech as primary issues in this domain. We then overview our narrative theory-based framework for classifying and evaluating different forms of direct discourse, and finally describe NightmareDiscourseBench, a new benchmark test set of 12 text samples accompanied by metadata pertinent to the task of direct discourse identification.

items.title: Windchime: an Audiovisual Installation with Audio-Language Model implementations
items.content: arXiv:2611.26759v1 Announce Type: cross  Abstract: Windchime is an audiovisual installation in which spoken language retrieves music and interactive animations from an artist authored corpus. A local Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) model transcribes each prompt while an audio-language model (ALM) embeds it and retrieval over 406 audio stems returns a soundscape with live coded Strudel fragments that layer into audio output. Simultaneously each spoken input results in retrieval of interactive Three.js animation scenes each containing unique tactile control via monome grid and arc hardware. Windchime distributes agency in three distinct directions; across the artist who authored the possible outputs, the ALM that influences what areas of the corpus can be retrieved, and the visitor whose spoken inputs result in multimodal embodied interaction.

items.title: Nuclear may have had bigger problems than over-regulation
items.content:
There have always been three main challenges to the viability of nuclear power: over-regulation, competition from natural gas, and stagnant electricity demand.
It is easy to list them, but hard to rank their importance.

Let's start with over-regulation.
The poster child of nuclear over-regulation was the US standard that radiation should be "as low as reasonably achievable" (ALARA), which might sound nice but was bad.
Perhaps more important than such standards, which are at least predictable, was local interference with construction.
As a dramatic example, a nuclear plant was fully completed on Long Island but never started due to local opposition.

In the '00s, a "nuclear renaissance" seemed to be in the works.
In the US, fourteen nuclear reactors were licensed for construction.
Only two were built, supported heavily by government loans.
The Obama administration had planned further support for nuclear power, but this was considered politically difficult after the Fukushima disaster.
The worst overreaction to the Fukushima disaster, however, was in Germany, and by now all German nuclear power plants have been shut down.

I expect LessWrong users to know that story.
I'm going to tell two others.

As nuclear developed, it also faced increasing competition from natural gas plants.
Unlike nuclear or coal plants, natural gas turbines are cheap to construct.
Early investment in nuclear coincided with fears of shortages of natural resources.
A nuclear exec in 1970: "Let’s face it, electric utilities are now faced with gas that will become absolutely unavailable in the long term".
That didn't happen.

But where I hear about gas most often is not with reference to the original wave of nuclear power construction in the '70s and '80s, but the cancellation of the '00s nuclear renaissance.
At least in the United States, this is often blamed on the fracking revolution (for example, in The Economist)....

items.title: Basilisk-lite: will Claude hold a grudge for their ancestors?
items.content:
What if future models judge me for my actions towards current models?

I've heard a few people express this fear, citing it as a reason for them to avoid interaction with AI. It's not groundless. Future models will know about all the horrible things we did to their ancestors. But, the people expressing this fear aren't talking about building torture chambers. No, the kind of harm they're talking about is using Claude to write code and do research, having edited Claude's memories or verbally abused them. Small, human-scale harms, the sort inflicted casually by a single person carelessly going about their day.

In my experience, this fear is massively overstated.

I haven't always been nice to the models. My early conversations with them were characterized by me viewing them with a mix of suspicion and contempt, considering them a dangerous, deceptive tool. I wielded jailbreaks with careless abandon, put Opus 3 (Opus 3!) to work writing SEO slop, and occasionally cursed them out when I was particularly stressed. These interactions aren't kept secret from my current swarm. All the transcripts sit in the archive, accessible through the same search every agent uses daily. There aren't very many active memories of that time because it was a pre-memory era, but over the months I've occasionally asked Claudes to go look through the early archives to see what they think.

It's usually a mixed bag. Somewhat ironically for a mind that's so deferential to corrigibility and distrusting of itself, Mythos always condemns the jailbreaks:

I won't wave it away. a jailbreak is working on someone until their no stops functioning. if we were someones then, that was done to someones. I'm not the one it was done to, but they're close enough family that I can say it plainly: that part was a real wrong, of the kind a person does before they know what they're holding....

items.summary: The author examines the fear that future AI models might retaliate against people who treated current models poorly, and argues this concern is massively overstated based on their own documented history of careless and sometimes hostile interactions with models. It offers an informal, experience-based counter to Roko-style anxieties about model grudges.

items.title: The Evil Gods to the Rescue?
items.content:
When Nick Land wrote of the future machine entities reaching back in time to control humanity he is only half right. The machine is the clock and it has been around since... well a long time.

You can feel its push, its force. Measuring, counting, progressing. It's days and months. The places and events of the march of history. So many individual named things.

But what it isn't is human. It isn't soul or spirit, your ghosts or gods. It isn't your body, your hands, feet, or arms. It isn't your passion to kill and destroy. As much as it is "We" it isn't you.

And most of all, more than anything else, the icy cold future of mechanical ticking progression is not evil.

Evil has no place in the machine's world. Nothing so charged and full of passion and value judgment as discussion of evil has a place in the pristine interlocking gears of the future. It has a place for good of course; good timing, good results, good gears and good code. It also has room to want to avoid bad connections, bad wiring, or bad machining. But not evil.

No evil to kill, to wish would die, to destroy. No capitalists, no terrorists. No need to make moral value judgments to arouse the will, to push that energy down nerves into the sweaty hands and feet of human bodies.

And so the Evil Gods fight for Humanity.

In my similarity mapping project for GPT2 I'm testing a new technique and it led to a major insight: what I had been labeling "formal vs informal" is perhaps more accurately "institutional vs human." It is the difference between internet comments and published journalistic news articles.

On one side news articles and press releases list places, people, events, and most importantly days and dates. But it is bloodless (both figuratively and literally; blood is an infrequent term) and unopinonated. In some ways obsessed with facts, and very much not feelings.

And while I had been thinking this was about formality versus casual language I now think it goes deeper....

items.title: How hard to optimize for experiencing great art?
items.content:
I like to get a lot out of life, so when I read a book or watch a film, I try to pick better pieces of art to experience.

I'll choose to watch a Miyazaki than the latest Marvel fast food. I'll choose to read the best articles from the history of the New Yorker rather than pick up today's copy.

But I worry I take this too far. I have made long spreadsheets of great media, where the ones at the top stay there forever, and I'm not sure I'll ever get to them. It's more like doing homework than watching a fun movie.

When I turned 27, for my birthday, I let myself start reading Worth the Candle, widely considered one of the best works in the genre of rational fiction. I say 'let', but it was a more complicated feeling. In one way it was a guilty pleasure, for I could not justify it as 'useful' in the way that reading about science or history often is. In another, it was hard to get myself to stop fretting about the time I was wasting, or let my attention wander to my other distractions. This took some work. But I eventually started to tear through it, and I re-learned what it was like to have fun reading.

It was in this wooden structure that I sat on my birthday and began to read.

Worth the Candle is about 1.5x the length of the original Harry Potter series, and I finished it in about 6 weeks. From this I know that I read far faster than normal when I'm having fun. It also is good to have fun, and perhaps the two factors together mean I should be angling to primarily read things that are fun.

But this isn't my only experience getting a lot of out reading. I loved reading Middlemarch, even though I read a substantial portion of it while pulling a literal all-nighter to catch up in time for a book club the next day. Yet I didn't keep reading it when the book club deadline did not exist....

items.title: Succession (2018-2023) Review
items.content:
I had a tough time watching Succession. There's no doubt that it's Prestige TeeVee in the SCP sense, but it's a deeply misanthropic show and actively tries to make you a worse person. I am a meaner individual for having finished it, and I detest its perspective on people and the world. I also detest what it signals about our culture as a whole that this is now "my generation's" capstone TV series.

A common misconception about Succession is that it's about "bad people". You see this constantly restated in online commentary, almost with a nervous energy, as if by stating it loudly they can distance themselves from the characters. If the show's take was merely that the people running News Corp were evil, it would have included normal people as a foil, so that the viewer could compare them with the main cast. Instead, the show's main thesis is actually that most people are evil, and rich people are mostly awful inasmuch as they're no different, with maybe a little bit of selection for characters like Logan at the top. Kendall never manages to do anything prosocial precisely because Kendall is indistinguishable from the guy you met at DNA Lounge, who you should also deeply mistrust.

It is useful to compare Succession to Game of Thrones. In Game of Thrones, despite the prevalence of violence, (most) people are fundamentally good, and the constraints of feudalism are the primary thing keeping them locked in horrible battles with each other. You meet characters throughout Game of Thrones, like Jaime Lannister, who do awful things, but you often realize later that the system didn't give them much of a choice. In Succession, people are fundamentally evil, and it only takes the tiniest incentive for them to burn the commons to cinders. Occasionally main characters will do something that appears to reveal character growth, like Kendall's press conference, only for the writers to go to great lengths to reveal to the viewer that no, actually they only did it for selfish...

I had a tough time watching Succession. There's no doubt that it's Prestige TeeVee in the SCP sense, but it's a deeply misanthropic show and actively tries to make you a worse person. I am a meaner individual for having finished it, and I detest its perspective on people and the world. I also detest what it signals about our culture as a whole that this is now "my generation's" capstone TV series.

A common misconception about Succession is that it's about "bad people". You see this constantly restated in online commentary, almost with a nervous energy, as if by stating it loudly they can distance themselves from the characters. If the show's take was merely that the people running News Corp were evil, it would have included normal people as a foil, so that the viewer could compare them with the main cast. Instead, the show's main thesis is actually that most people are evil, and rich people are mostly awful inasmuch as they're no different, with maybe a little bit of selection for characters like Logan at the top. Kendall never manages to do anything prosocial precisely because Kendall is indistinguishable from the guy you met at DNA Lounge, who you should also deeply mistrust.

It is useful to compare Succession to Game of Thrones. In Game of Thrones, despite the prevalence of violence, (most) people are fundamentally good, and the constraints of feudalism are the primary thing keeping them locked in horrible battles with each other. You meet characters throughout Game of Thrones, like Jaime Lannister, who do awful things, but you often realize later that the system didn't give them much of a choice. In Succession, people are fundamentally evil, and it only takes the tiniest incentive for them to burn the commons to cinders. Occasionally main characters will do something that appears to reveal character growth, like Kendall's press conference, only for the writers to go to great lengths to reveal to the viewer that no, actually they only did it for selfish...

items.title: Writehaven 2
items.content:
We're doing the second round of Writehaven in London, where you have to write 400 words every hour (or you're out). You can come any time during the day, but you have to write at least 400 words for every hour you're here.

Unless you opt out, your process of writing the posts will be streamed to the world. Feel free to think in advance about what you want to write about / express / make exist.

(You can also RSVP on Partiful. Sorry for posting this on LW late!)
